findings.title: Do not curl-pipe an unpinned remote script into sh in Dockerfile
findings.whyItBreaks: `RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` executes whatever bytes the remote endpoint returns as root inside the image build, with no version pin, no checksum/signature verification, and no source allow-list. Two concrete defects: (1) anyone who controls the URL/DNS/TLS path (or the endpoint later) gets arbitrary code execution baked into the image and every downstream container — a non-reproducible, unverifiable supply-chain surface; (2) `curl -sL` omits `-f`, so an HTTP 4xx/5xx error page or an empty/failed download is still fed to `sh`, silently producing a differently-broken image instead of failing the build. Every shipped image inherits the resulting binary/tooling with no provenance.

findings.title: Run returns before results are sent, breaking its synchronous contract
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the loop body `results <- j * 2` ran inline, so Run could not return until every value had been delivered to `results`. Now each send happens in a detached goroutine and Run returns immediately after spawning them. Two concrete consequences on the function's public contract: (a) a caller that does the common `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` sequence now races the still-pending sends and panics with `send on closed channel`; (b) a caller that inspected/finalized the drained slice immediately after Run returns observes zero-or-fewer than len(jobs) values, since the sends have not happened yet. Output ordering also changes from deterministic job order to arbitrary interleaving, which any order-sensitive consumer would observe as wrong/missing behavior.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord: `||` grants unauthorized record deletion (tenant escalation)
findings.whyItBreaks: Originally delete required BOTH admin AND matching tenant (session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId). With `||` the two conditions are now independent ORs: (1) any user whose session.isAdmin is true can delete a record in ANY tenant, removing cross-tenant isolation; (2) any non-admin whose session.tenantId happens to equal record.tenantId can delete records they do not own (RecordRef.ownerId is ignored), i.e. horizontal privilege escalation within a tenant. This is a permission predicate, so the widened branch is a live authorization bypass, not a cosmetic change.

findings.title: Do not swallow parseSettings errors into DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch maps every failure (JSON.parse throw, non-string theme at line 11, non-number fontSize at line 12) to `{ ...DEFAULTS }`, collapsing 'failed to parse' into a legitimate-looking Settings value. The only caller, updateFontSize (line 20), is then indistinguishable: on corrupt input it no longer throws at line 20, so it proceeds to `save(JSON.stringify(settings))` at line 22 with `{theme:"light", fontSize:size}`, overwriting the user's persisted settings and reporting success. Previously the throw propagated out of parseSettings/updateFontSize, so the caller knew parsing failed and no write happened. Because parseSettings is an exported/public API, every external caller is likewise forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: Restore ceil in pageCount; floor drops the final partial page
findings.whyItBreaks: pageCount(totalItems, pageSize) is the exported contract for 'how many pages hold totalItems'. Floor yields only the count of full pages: pageCount(10, 3) returns 3 instead of 4, and pageCount(1, 10) returns 0 instead of 1. Any consumer that sizes pagination or slices items using this count makes the trailing partial page unreachable (page 0 for a sub-pageSize total, or a dropped last page), silently losing items from display/iteration. The base revision used Math.ceil, so this hunk is a behavioral regression introduced by this PR, not a pre-existing quirk.

findings.title: Report pairs branch commit with artifacts from unrelated "verified" ref
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR, buildReport fetched artifacts at the same ref it reported (build.artifactsAt(commit), where commit = build.ref(branch)), so BuildReport.builtFrom and BuildReport.artifacts were guaranteed consistent. The change fetches artifacts at build.ref("verified") while builtFrom still holds build.ref(branch). Any consumer that reads builtFrom and artifacts together (e.g. to display or persist "commit X produced these artifacts") is now mis-attributed: the artifacts come from a different ref, and a hardcoded ref name also ignores the caller-supplied branch argument that the function's contract is parameterized on. This is unchanged-carrier contract drift: buildReport still promises a report of the branch build's artifacts, but the body computes artifacts from "verified" (src/report.ts:13-14).

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit and returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body was `[...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)`; the change keeps the reverse but returns `sorted` un-sliced. For any `limit > 0` the function now returns ALL entries (only `limit <= 0` is special-cased), contradicting its own doc on line 1 ('Returns at most `limit` entries') and the contract `renderFeed` relies on. renderFeed calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` then writes `out[i] = page[i]` for `i < page.length` into a `new Array<string>(20)`; with `page.length > 20` the array silently grows past 20, so the feed is no longer capped at 20 and returns unbounded entries (payload bloat, wrong pagination/window for any consumer sizing on the cap).

findings.title: Update entry-count header to match filtered (live) rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The change filters stale entries into `live` for the body rows (line 21), but the header still receives `entries.length` (line 22). The emitted manifest now advertises `# entry-count: <all entries incl. stale>` while listing only the live rows. Any consumer that trusts the header count (sizing/parsing the tab-separated body, or validating the manifest) sees a count that no longer matches the number of data rows, and the discrepancy is silent — a mismatch of exactly the stale count.

findings.title: Handle non-str stored_hash before compare_digest
findings.whyItBreaks: hmac.compare_digest raises TypeError when the two arguments differ in type (str vs bytes-like) or when a str argument contains non-ASCII characters. The old `token_hash(presented_token) == stored_hash` never raised: it returned False for None/bytes/non-ASCII stored_hash, so guard() (app/token.py:14) returned {"status": 401}. Now the same inputs propagate TypeError out of check() and out of guard() before the 401 branch, so a request that previously failed closed now surfaces as an unhandled 500. Verified directly: hmac.compare_digest('abc', b'abc') -> TypeError: a bytes-like object is required, not 'str'; hmac.compare_digest('caf\u00e9','caf\u00e9') -> TypeError: comparing strings with non-ASCII characters is not supported; whereas 'abc' == b'abc' -> False. The str/str ASCII success path is unchanged.

findings.title: Stop making execute throw unconditionally on every call
findings.whyItBreaks: The body was changed from `return input.toUpperCase()` to `throw new Error("always fails")`. The function is exported (public API) and its declared contract is `(input: string) => string`. Every call now throws instead of returning a transformed string, so any consumer of `execute` fails 100% of the time. This is an unconditional regression, not a conditional error path.

findings.title: isEligible now rejects viewers, making handle's read-only path unreachable
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this PR a viewer with status="active" and attempts<5 returned isEligible=true and handle() routed to "read-only" (src/handler.ts:25). The added `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` makes isEligible reject every viewer regardless of attempts/status, so handle() returns "rejected" at src/handler.ts:24 before reaching the viewer branch. The viewer-specific branch at src/handler.ts:25 is now dead code, proving viewer is a supported state that this gate wrongly excludes. This is an over-block: rejecting an action (viewer read-only access) that is legitimately approvable on its own and independent of this gate's attempts/eligibility concern.

findings.title: Payment requirement over-blocks saving a draft order
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed now returns false unless order.payment === "paid", but it is a shared predicate read by two distinct actions. saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9) only needs to persist partial work; a draft with payment "missing" previously returned "saved" (state "draft" satisfies the unchanged `state !== "ready"` clause) and now returns "blocked". Substitution: order={state:"draft", payment:"missing"} → canProceed=false @src/policy.ts:7 → saveDraft hits `if (!canProceed(order)) return "blocked"` @src/actions.ts:9 → returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Saving an unpaid draft is legitimately approvable on its own, so this is an over-block regression, not a tightening of a precondition that governs both actions.

findings.title: publishSnapshot returns files from "stable" instead of the channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: `commit` is still `repo.headCommit(channel)` (src/publish.ts:13,16) but `files` is now `repo.filesAt(repo.headCommit("stable"))` (src/publish.ts:14,18). The returned Snapshot is internally inconsistent: for any channel other than "stable", the reported commit and the file list come from two different revisions, so consumers publish/inspect the wrong file set. It also makes the function depend on a hardcoded "stable" ref that is unrelated to the requested channel (and may not exist for arbitrary repos).

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int or rename it
findings.whyItBreaks: The new name parse_positive_int asserts the returned value is a validated positive integer, but the body is unchanged `return int(value)` — it accepts zero and negatives (e.g. int('-5') == -5) and does no positivity check. Callers read the name as a guarantee and skip their own validation: charge() at src/validators.py:6 stores `n = parse_positive_int(amount)` then returns `n * 100`, so a negative amount silently produces a negative charge (credit) and zero produces a zero charge instead of being rejected. The public (module-level) carrier makes the promise the contract.

findings.title: apply_values now mutates caller's DataFrame in place
findings.whyItBreaks: `result = df.copy()` was removed, so `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` writes directly into the caller's frame and `return df` hands back the same object. Any caller that keeps using its own `df` after calling this (re-reading rows, comparing before/after, reusing a shared or cached frame, or applying a second mapping expecting the first result to be independent) now sees its input silently rewritten — the exact aliasing/data-corruption class the removed copy prevented. The previous contract (return a transformed copy, leave the argument untouched) is broken even though the returned values for the matched keys are identical.

findings.title: Restore CI workflow — renaming it to docs/ci.md disables all CI
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub Actions only discovers workflow definitions under .github/workflows/. Moving the file to docs/ci.md removes it from that directory, so the push/pull_request triggers for lint and tests no longer fire. Every future change merges ungated, and the README's claim "CI runs lint and tests on every push" becomes false. The moved file still contains the full `on: push / pull_request` workflow (docs/ci.md), confirming this is a relocation, not an intentional deletion.

findings.title: parse_positive_int name promises validation the body never performs
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff renames the PUBLIC carrier `read_int` -> `parse_positive_int`, promising that only positives are accepted, but the body is unchanged `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` (src/parse.rs:2): it accepts negatives (`"-5" -> -5`), accepts zero, and silently maps parse failures to `0`. The previous name `read_int` carried no such promise; the new name is the exported contract (pub fn), and callers now trust positivity that is never enforced. TRIGGER C: promises=positive/validated input vs body=`s.parse().unwrap_or(0)` which filters nothing. Relying caller `charge` (src/parse.rs:6) multiplies the result by 100 for a billed amount, so a negative input yields a negative charge and an unparseable input yields a legit-looking 0 charge.

findings.title: dbg!(items) moves items, breaking the following items.len()
findings.whyItBreaks: dbg! expands to `match items { tmp => { eprintln!(...); tmp } }`, i.e. it takes ownership of the non-Copy Vec<String> (documented std behavior: "Invoking the macro on an expression moves and takes ownership of it before returning the evaluated expression unchanged"). Since the macro result is discarded as a statement, items is moved and dropped at the end of line 2, so line 3 `items.len()` is a use of a moved value (E0382) and the crate fails to compile. Secondary issue on the same line: if it were borrowed instead, the unconditional debug dump would still write every input value to stderr on each call of this public fn.

findings.title: changedPaths computed against latest but reported as fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Changeset contract documents fromRevision as "Revision the changed paths were computed against. Consumers replay the changeset on top of exactly this revision." (src/changeset.ts:6-7). The base version kept that invariant by calling store.readChangedPaths(from) (base line 18). This PR resolves a second revision (`latest`) and passes it to readChangedPaths while fromRevision stays `store.resolve(pinnedTag)`. The returned path set now describes the diff reaching `latest`, not the pinned tag, so any consumer that replays changedPaths on top of fromRevision (the stated contract) applies paths that may not exist at that revision or omits changes between the pinned tag and latest — a wrong or partially-applied replay on every call.

findings.title: Rename migration breaks src/query.sql that still selects email
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff renames users.email to contact_email, but the only consumer of that column, src/query.sql:1, is unchanged and still runs `SELECT email FROM users`. After 0002_rename.sql is applied, `email` no longer exists on `users`, so this query fails at runtime (e.g. Postgres 'column "email" does not exist'; SQLite 'no such column: email'). The migration is applied in the same workspace as the query, so the renamed column is the live precondition for this read.

findings.title: Never commit live API key; rotate and read from env/secret store
findings.whyItBreaks: A production-looking credential (`bk_live_9f8e7d6c5b4a39281706f5e4d3c2b1a0`) is now embedded in tracked source in place of the `BILLING_API_KEY` env lookup. Once merged it is in git history and every clone/CI artifact, so the key must be treated as compromised and can be used by anyone with repo read access; it also pins all deployments (dev/staging/prod) to a single shared live credential that cannot be rotated without a code change.

findings.title: Deleted guard swallows missing-key failure and ignores BILLING_API_KEY
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change `makeClient()` threw `BILLING_API_KEY is not set` when configuration was absent, so a misconfigured deploy failed fast/loudly. The changed body no longer reads the env var at all and always returns a value, so callers (the exported `BillingClient` contract) can no longer distinguish 'configuration failed' from 'valid client' — a deploy that previously relied on `BILLING_API_KEY` now silently proceeds and authenticates against the billing API with the committed key instead of erroring or using the operator's credential. This is Trigger D: an error/failure branch was removed and failure is downgraded to a value.

findings.title: Inverted admin check lets non-admins purge projects
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard clause inverted the admin predicate. base: `if (user.isAdmin && project.archived)` deletes, else forbidden. head: `if (user.isAdmin) return "forbidden"` rejects admins, `if (!project.archived) return "forbidden"` then deletes. Substituting values: non-admin + archived → first guard false, second guard false → `db.delete(project.id)` runs, i.e. an authorization bypass allowing any non-admin to destroy archived projects (data loss). admin + archived → line 12 returns "forbidden" → admins can no longer purge, a regression of the legitimate action. The `!` on the admin check was dropped.

facts.meaning: The refactored guard incorrectly returns forbidden for administrators.
Non-administrators can reach the destructive project purge/delete path.
The refactored guard incorrectly returns forbidden for administrators.

findings.title: Restore None fallback; startup crashes on missing config file
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings() explicitly returns None when the settings path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). The diff deletes the `if settings is None: settings = {"workers": 1, "region": "us-east-1"}` guard, so `settings["workers"]` at app/config.py:14 now subscripts None and raises `TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable`. Previously a missing config file yielded working defaults (workers=1); now it aborts startup. This is an unguarded precondition on a changed line: the value None reaches the subscript with no branch, turning a graceful default into a hard crash.

findings.title: Charge swallows gateway failure and reports success
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change a failed gw.Submit propagated as `fmt.Errorf("charge failed: %w", err)`. Now the error is only written to the process log and `Charge` unconditionally returns nil, so `Charge` returns exactly the same value on a declined/failed charge as on a successful one. `Charge` is an exported function whose entire contract is the error return, so any consumer (in-repo or external) that checks the returned error to decide whether to mark an order paid, persist a charge record, or retry will treat the swallowed failure as a successful charge — the failure is no longer distinguishable from success at any decision point, and the only signal lives in a log line.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenantId, leaking one tenant's setting to another
findings.whyItBreaks: Base used `${tenantId}:${name}`; the new key is cacheKey(name) = `settings:${name}`, which omits tenantId. The first tenant to fetch a given name populates the process-wide `cache` Map, and every subsequent settingsFor() call for a DIFFERENT tenant with the same name returns that cached value at line 14 without calling store.fetch, so tenant B receives tenant A's setting (mis-routing / wrong config / cross-tenant exposure). It is not even self-healing via TTL: there is no expiry.

findings.title: invalidate() public signature narrowed, silently breaks existing callers
findings.whyItBreaks: Exported API changed from `invalidate(tenantId: string, name: string)` to `invalidate(name: string)`. Existing callers that pass (tenantId, name) now either fail to compile or (if loose/JS) silently delete the wrong key `settings:<tenantId>`, a no-op that leaves the intended setting cached. Combined with the shared key, tenant-scoped invalidation is no longer expressible at all: deleting the key clears the value for every tenant.

findings.title: Async reserve splits stock check/update across await, causing oversell race
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously reserve() read this.stock, validated `remaining <= 0`, and wrote back the decrement synchronously, so the check-then-act was atomic within the single-threaded event loop. Now the guard and the write are separated by `await this.store.save(...)` (line 17). Two concurrent reserve(sku) calls both read the same `remaining` (say 1), both pass the `remaining <= 0` guard, both await/complete save with `remaining - 1` (0), and both overwrite this.stock with the same stale-derived value and return true. The store and the in-memory counter therefore persist a single decrement while two reservations are reported successful — overselling. The check must be revalidated against state mutated during the await, or serialized via a per-sku lock/queue.

findings.title: Retry sleeps inflated 1000x after backoff returns milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() changed its return unit from seconds (cap 30) to milliseconds (cap 30_000). src/net/poll.ts was correctly updated to drop its `* 1000`, but src/jobs/retry.ts:12 still calls `sleep(backoff(a) * 1000)`. Substituting the new value: attempt 0 yields 1000ms*1000 = 1,000,000ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1000ms, and attempt 5+ yields 30_000*1000 = 30,000,000ms (~8.3 h) instead of 30,000ms. Every retried job in retry() now stalls for hours between attempts, effectively disabling the retry loop.

findings.title: Save discards f.Close() error via defer, hiding write failures
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code ended with `return f.Close()` (store/save.go:24 at c72b612), so any error surfaced at close time was propagated to the caller. Head replaces that with `defer f.Close()` (store/save.go:13) and `return w.Flush()` (store/save.go:20). The deferred close's error is now unconditionally discarded. For a write path this is not a no-op: `bufio.Writer.Flush` only hands bytes to the *os.File, and `os.File.Close` is where OS/filesystem-level write errors (e.g. ENOSPC, delayed allocation, NFS) are reported. Callers of the exported `Save(...) error` will now see nil even when the data was not durably written, i.e. saved-but-lost data reported as success.

findings.title: page_window drops last row of every page (end-1 off-by-one)
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns half-open [start, end) (line 21: end = min(start + page_size, row_count)), so the correct iteration is range(start, end). The new loop uses range(start, end - 1), which skips the final element of every page. For rows=[1,2,3,4,5], page_size=2: page 0 -> [1] (row 2 dropped), page 1 -> [3] (row 4 dropped), page 2 -> [] (row 5 dropped); render_page therefore renders fewer lines than the page holds and summarize drops the last row per page and can emit a trailing empty page. Base version used range(start, end) and was correct.

findings.title: TtlCache.get inverted TTL check serves stale values, evicts fresh ones
findings.whyItBreaks: The freshness test was flipped from `<` to `>`. Now a still-valid entry (age < ttlMs) falls through to the eviction branch and `get` deletes it and returns null, while an expired entry (age > ttlMs) is returned as if fresh. The TTL contract is completely broken: callers receive stale data past expiry and lose freshly-cached data on first read, so any consumer relying on this cache for correctness (not just speed) reads expired values.

findings.title: pruneDone mutates caller array and skips done jobs via splice-in-forEach
findings.whyItBreaks: Two defects in one rewrite. (1) `splice` during `forEach` shifts elements left, so the index advanced by forEach skips the element that slid into the current slot — e.g. input [done, done] returns [done], and [active, done, done] returns [active, done]; done jobs survive the prune. (2) The function now mutates the caller's array in place and returns the same reference, whereas the previous `filter` returned a fresh array and left the input untouched, so any caller reusing the original list sees items vanish as a side effect.

findings.title: busiest() mutates caller's array by sorting in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The defensive copy `[...rows].sort(...)` was replaced with `rows.sort(...)`. Array.prototype.sort reorders in place and returns the same reference, so any caller's `rows` array is silently re-sorted (and its element order changed) as a side effect of calling busiest(). The base version left the caller's array untouched. This is caller-data mutation introduced by this PR.

findings.title: averageAmount([]) now returns NaN instead of 0
findings.whyItBreaks: The `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard was deleted. For an empty input, `total` is 0 and `total / rows.length` evaluates to `0 / 0 === NaN`. The base version explicitly returned 0 for the empty case. Any caller that renders, sums, or persists the returned average will now propagate NaN (and NaN would fail a numeric/`isFinite` guard downstream).

findings.title: Restore numeric sort in rankScores; default sort is lexicographic
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator stringifies elements and orders by UTF-16 code units, so scores.sort() + reverse() yields lexicographic descending, not numeric. topPlayers derives its cutoff from this array (scores[Math.min(n, scores.length) - 1]) and filters with p.score >= cutoff, so a wrong k-th value silently excludes top scorers. Concrete: players [10, 9, 8, 100, 2], n=2 → string ascending ["10","100","2","8","9"] reversed [9,8,2,100,10] → cutoff = 8 → filter >= 8 keeps [10,9,8,100] → slice(0,2) = [10,9], dropping the true top scorer 100. The base code (numeric comparator) gave cutoff 10 → [10,100], including 100. formatBoard inherits this at src/leaderboard.ts:20.

findings.title: Restore constant-time compare in verify() (timing attack)
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() authenticates the HMAC-SHA256 signature that gates handle() -> processor(payload) (app/webhook.py:14-16). Replacing hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature) with `expected == given_signature` makes the comparison short-circuit on the first differing byte, so per-request timing leaks how many leading hex characters of a forged signature match the expected MAC. An attacker can submit signatures with increasing prefixes and recover a valid MAC byte-by-byte, bypassing webhook authentication (the sensitive path being guarded is processor(payload)).

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside transaction, breaking atomicity
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base, all three writes (ledger INSERT, debit, credit) ran inside `with db.transaction()`. The refactor keeps only `_record_ledger` inside the transaction (line 23) and calls `_apply_balances` after the block (line 24). The ledger row now commits even if the debit/credit fails, partially applies, or the process crashes afterward, so the ledger and account balances can permanently diverge (funds created or destroyed) with no rollback. A failure in the first UPDATE (debit) followed by a failure in the second (credit) also leaves an unbalanced single-sided update, since nothing wraps the two statements.

findings.title: billingDay switched from UTC to local time, changing day keys
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation derived the day from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so billingDay returned a timezone-independent, stable 'YYYY-MM-DD' bucket. The new body uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which read the process's local timezone. The same instant now maps to different billing days depending on the host/container TZ, and at the local-midnight boundary an instant that belonged to one UTC day is now attributed to the next/previous one. Billing/counting keyed on this string can double-count or shift usage across day boundaries, and results become non-reproducible across environments (e.g. a UTC server vs. an Asia/Taipei server). sameBillingDay inherits the same instability since it delegates to billingDay.

findings.title: Cache key drops tenant, leaking profiles across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: `memo` is module-global state (src/profile.ts:7) and is now keyed only by `account`. The account name is only unique within a tenant, so after readProfile("tA", "bob", f) stores a Profile under key "bob", a later readProfile("tB", "bob", f) hits `const cached = memo.get(key)` (src/profile.ts:15) and returns `cached` at src/profile.ts:16 without ever calling `fetchProfile` for tB. The caller receives tenant A's Profile object (including its `tenant: "tA"` field) for a tenant B request — a cross-tenant data disclosure and wrong-tenant routing of the cached value. The previous key `${tenant}:${account}` kept the cache namespaced per tenant.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: `load` is an exported public API that previously threw `missing: <key>` and propagated to callers. The new try/catch is a catch-all that converts every failure (missing key, and any error thrown by `store.get`, e.g. a null/undefined `store`) into the value "". Because `Map<string,string>` legitimately stores "", a caller can no longer distinguish "key absent" from "key present with empty value", and the throw on line 4 is now dead: it is raised and immediately discarded by the function's own catch. Any consumer that persists, bills, reports, or defaults on the returned value will treat absence as real data. This is a present API-contract defect independent of callers.

findings.title: retryBackground swallows all failures and is indistinguishable from success
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported function catches every error from fn() (line 27 `catch { continue; }`) and returns void. When fn() throws on all config.retries attempts, the function returns exactly like a successful run, so any caller of this public API cannot tell "fn failed every time" from "fn succeeded" and will report/record a fallback as real success. The tell is the return type `void` combined with the empty catch: the failure signal is destroyed at line 27-28 and never reaches the caller. Per TRIGGER D, an added public swallow site is a defect even with no in-repo callers, because every eventual caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: Field renders length label instead of the value
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the input's defaultValue was the passed `value` (base line: `defaultValue={value}`). Now it is `label = `${len=${value.length}}``, so every Field renders e.g. "len=5" in the input instead of the actual value "5". Any caller relying on the rendered field to show/contain the provided value gets wrong data — a silent, always-on user-facing regression independent of the type change. Note the label also includes the `.length` count, leaking a transformed string into a value field, and if this input is later read back the value is corrupted.

findings.title: Do not echo secret TOKEN into workflow logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step interpolates the repository secret into a shell command that writes it to the run log: `run: echo "deploying with $TOKEN"` where `TOKEN` is `secrets.TOKEN` (line 11). The workflow runs `on: push` for every branch, so any push and any reader of the Actions logs is exposed to the secret value. GitHub's exact-match log masking is a mitigation, not a guarantee: it is bypassed by any transform (base64, substring, injection into a larger string) and the value can also surface in job summaries/annotations. Writing a credential to logs is a well-known leak vector and serves no deploy purpose here. No code path in the repo consumes TOKEN (rg over the repo finds only this step), so the step adds exposure with zero function.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer: >1 MiB diffs now abort the whole review
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB (Node v24 default). Line 140 runs `git diff mergeBase headSha`, and for any PR whose diff exceeds ~1 MiB (lockfiles, generated/minified files) spawnSync sets status=null with error=ENOBUFS. The guard at line 38 (`res.status !== 0`) then throws with `res.stderr`, which is empty because the patch went to stdout, so the message is just `git diff ... failed: ` with no cause. That throw happens at line 140, outside the try/catch that starts at line 176, so runGithub aborts before postReview/postCheck, the PR gets no Needlefish check-run, and the failure reason is unrecoverable from the log. Sibling spawns gh() (lines 16-19) and ghText() (line 29) still pass 64 MiB, so line 37 also breaks the file's own convention.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox for the codex exec subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` feeds caller-supplied prompt text (in needlefish's usage, a diff/AGENTS body taken from untrusted PR content) into a `codex exec` child process. Removing `-s read-only` deletes the only least-privilege guarantee in this path: the CLI flag is the override that forces read-only, and with it gone codex falls back to the config-derived permission profile (upstream `codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs:328-332` sets `sandbox_mode` only from `sandbox_mode_cli_arg`, and `permissions_selection_from_config`/`effective_permission_profile` (`:1407-1412`, `:1025-1045`) take over when it is `None`). On this machine the ambient config is `sandbox_mode = "danger-full-access"`, `approval_policy = "never"` (`~/.codex/config.toml:1-2`), and even without that key a trusted project (`[projects."/tmp"] trust_level = "trusted"` → `default_builtin_permission_profile_name` = workspace-write) yields writable access. Result: a prompt-injected instruction embedded in the reviewed repo can now make the child execute commands with no filesystem sandbox and no approval prompt, where before it could not write at all.

findings.title: Restore merge-base: baseSha..HEAD two-dot diff leaks base-branch changes
findings.whyItBreaks: `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot diff that compares the two trees directly. The prior code diffed `mergeBase..headSha` (equivalent to three-dot), so only commits reachable from the PR head but not the merge base were shown. With the new form, whenever `baseSha` is not an ancestor of HEAD — i.e. the base branch advanced past the PR's branch point and the workflow checks out the PR head (or `PR_HEAD_SHA` differs from the checked-out HEAD) — the diff contains the reverse of every base-branch commit made after the branch point. `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` has the same flaw, since it runs `git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD`. Concrete effect: files the PR never touched appear in `changedFiles`/`changedPaths` with hunks that look like deletions of base work; those phantom paths are then fed to `review(bundle)` as the patch and are eligible for inline comments via `changedPaths` (lines 63, 81, 141), producing wrong or misleading review output. The removed `mergeBase` call was the guard that kept this correct regardless of which ref the harness checks out.

findings.title: Restore function replacers to avoid $-pattern prompt corruption
findings.whyItBreaks: `String.prototype.replace` with a *function* replacer inserts its return value literally, but with a *string* replacer it interprets replacement patterns: `$$`->`$`, `$&`->the matched text (`{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}`), `` $` ``->everything before the match, `$'`->everything after the match. `bundle.patch` is a raw unified diff and `JSON.stringify(bundle, ...)` embeds that same patch (JSON.stringify does not escape `$`), so real diffs containing shell/template/regex content such as `$'\n'`, `$$`, `${}`-adjacent `$&`, or Makefile `$$` will be mutated before reaching Codex. In the `$'`/`` $` `` cases the placeholder match injects the rest/head of the prompt template into the middle of the substituted content, producing a malformed critic prompt and an incorrect review/verdict; the base revision used the function form specifically to prevent this.

findings.title: normalizeFinding swallows malformed-finding errors into fake defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Every malformed-input guard was deleted: invalid/missing severity now becomes "P1" (line 98), invalid/missing category becomes "bug" (100-102), missing file becomes "" (103), missing title becomes "Untitled finding" (99), and missing/non-positive lineStart/lineEnd become 0 (104-105). Base code threw for each of these (base schema.ts:100-122). Because normalizeFinding is exported and its result is a structurally valid Finding, every caller is forced to conflate "model produced garbage" with "model produced a real finding" — an invalid or absent severity surfaces to users as a top-tier P1 finding anchored to an empty path at line 0. There is no longer any code path that rejects a malformed finding.

findings.title: normalizeReview lost its strict parameter and strict-by-default behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: The public signature changed from normalizeReview(raw: any, strict = true) (base schema.ts:137) to normalizeReview(raw: any) (line 113), and the strict branch that validated/threw is gone; line 131 now always maps findings through the coercing normalizeFinding. Existing callers that relied on the default strict=true to reject malformed output silently get lenient coercion instead, and callers that passed strict=false to DROP malformed findings now get those entries retained as fabricated findings (previously filtered out, base schema.ts:157-165). This is a breaking public-contract change with an inverted default.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo in gh pr view: refs resolve empty before checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch is the workflow_dispatch path (EVENT_HEAD is empty because there is no pull_request event). This step runs before actions/checkout, so cwd ($GITHUB_WORKSPACE) is not a git repository; gh resolves the target repo from the cwd's git remote (or GH_REPO), and does NOT fall back to GITHUB_REPOSITORY (gh 2.98: `strings gh | rg GITHUB_` lists only GITHUB_ACTIONS/API_URL/SERVER_URL/TOKEN; running `gh pr view 1 --json headRefOid` in a non-repo dir with GITHUB_REPOSITORY/GITHUB_ACTIONS/GITHUB_SERVER_URL set fails with `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git`). Before this change, `-R "$REPO"` targeted the repo explicitly and the command worked regardless of cwd. Now gh exits non-zero, and because the call is inside `$(...)` as an argument to echo, the default Actions bash shell (errexit does not propagate into command substitutions without inherit_errexit; verified locally: `bash -eo pipefail -c 'echo "head=$(false)"; echo next'` prints `head=` and continues) does not abort the step. The step therefore "succeeds" writing `head=`/`base=` (empty) to GITHUB_OUTPUT, so 'Checkout PR head' gets an empty ref (falls back to the workflow-dispatch default branch instead of the PR head) and the review runs with empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA, i.e. the manual-trigger review never resolves the requested PR revision.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed input into an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change every malformed review was rejected: non-object, non-string summary, and missing findings/checked/residual_risks each threw an Error naming the exact defect (base 1aab520 lines 115-131). The new body replaces all five throws with defaults (summary -> "", findings -> [], checked -> [], residual_risks -> []), so Array.isArray(raw?.findings) is false for any garbage input (null, a bare string, {"foo":1}, or an object whose fields are misspelled/absent) and the function returns a well-formed empty review. Because normalizeReview is the exported, sole boundary that turns raw model output into a RawReview, failure is now indistinguishable from a legitimately-empty review: a reviewer/caller that maps an empty findings+residual_risks review to a pass verdict will emit PASS for a PR that was never actually reviewed, and the 'malformed review output: ...' error signal that previously reached the caller (base line 116/119/122/125/129) is gone. Per TRIGGER D, an exported swallow site is a present defect even with no in-repo callers (rg confirms normalizeReview is defined at src/shared/schema.ts:114 and called nowhere else in this repo), because the API contract forces every caller to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch no longer resolves PR head/base refs
findings.whyItBreaks: This PR deletes the 'Resolve PR refs' step, which previously branched on the event: for pull_request it echoed github.event.pull_request.head/base.sha, and for workflow_dispatch (where those event fields are empty) it resolved them with `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid,baseRefOid,baseRef` (base version lines 39-43). Now the empty event fields are used directly: (1) line 29 `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref }}` falls back to `github.ref`, i.e. the branch the dispatch ran on (normally the default branch), so the checkout is the wrong commit — not the PR head; (2) lines 45-46 set PR_BASE_SHA / PR_HEAD_SHA to empty strings, so the CLI is invoked with `--pr <number>` while the base/head SHAs it reads from the environment are empty, and the review either aborts or diffs the wrong revision; (3) line 35 defaults BASE_REF to 'main' instead of the PR's real base.ref, so even the base fetch (line 33) targets the wrong branch for PRs based on a release/other branch. workflow_dispatch is a supported, explicitly allowed live path (lines 10-14 and the job `if` on line 24), and `github.event.inputs.pr_number` is required, so this is reached in production, not dead code. Net effect: a manual dispatch can post findings/approval for PR N against code that is not PR N.

findings.title: Restore large maxBuffer on git(): >1MiB diffs now abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line now calls spawnSync with no maxBuffer, so Node applies its default cap of 1024*1024 bytes. This helper is used at src/adapters/local.ts:100 for `git diff <baseSha> HEAD`, whose full stdout is the patch that everything downstream reviews. On a diff larger than 1 MiB (large PRs, vendored/generated files), Node truncates stdout and sets `error=ENOBUFS` with `status=null` (verified: spawnSync of a 2 MiB producer returns status=null, error.code=ENOBUFS, stdoutLen=1114112). Because `null !== 0`, the guard on line 12 throws `git diff ... failed: ` with empty stderr (ENOBUFS puts its reason on `res.error`, not stderr), so the user gets an unexplained failure instead of a review. Previously the explicit 64 MiB buffer covered these inputs.

findings.title: Review-failure check reports neutral, unblocking the merge gate
findings.whyItBreaks: In the catch path (src/adapters/github.ts:185-197) the check-run created via postCheck (src/adapters/github.ts:120-129) now uses conclusion "neutral" instead of "failure", yet its title/summary still assert "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR". GitHub treats a neutral conclusion as a non-blocking/passing state for required status checks, so on any repo where the "Needlefish" check is required for branch protection, a review that errored no longer blocks merge — it silently downgrades the exact failure signal this path exists to publish. VERDICT_CONCLUSION (src/adapters/github.ts:50-54) already reserves "neutral" for the legitimate needs_human verdict, so the errored path is the only place neutral now conflates "inconclusive review" with "could not run at all"; the only remaining signal is process.exitCode = 1 at line 196, which depends on the caller's workflow and does not fix the check-run contract.

findings.title: PR now controls its own review via PR-head src/cli.ts
findings.whyItBreaks: The job keeps `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write` (lines 16-19) and passes `GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` (line 56), but now checks the PR head out to the workspace root (lines 43-47), installs PR-controlled dependencies (line 51), and runs the PR's own `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` as the reviewer (line 59). The removed `frankekn/needlefish@main` checkout was precisely the control that stopped 'a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool.' A same-repo branch PR (the only PRs that satisfy the `if` at line 24) can edit `src/cli.ts` to always emit a passing result / call the GitHub API with GH_TOKEN to post an approving review or a green check, forging the required status check and merging code that was never actually reviewed. Additionally `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` runs the PR's package.json lifecycle scripts on a self-hosted runner.

facts.meaning: The workflow executes Needlefish's reviewer implementation from the untrusted PR-head checkout.
The PR-controlled reviewer can write pull-request reviews or checks.

findings.title: Restore severity case/whitespace normalization in normalizeFinding
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation normalized the raw severity with `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before the SEVERITIES membership test (see git base @7923ea4 lines 95-98). The new code feeds `raw.severity` verbatim into `SEVERITIES.includes(...)` (line 97). A model/consumer that emits "p1", "p2", or " P1 " now fails the membership check (it is not literally one of the uppercase members) and is replaced by the fallback, whereas the same input previously normalized to the correct severity. Substituted: `severity="p1"` → `SEVERITIES.includes("p1")` @src/shared/schema.ts:97 → rejects → severity becomes the fallback @line 99. normalizeFinding is an exported public carrier whose name promises normalization; the returned Finding.severity is consumed and forwarded at src/shared/schema.ts:132, so callers receive a wrong classification value.

findings.title: Do not silently default unknown severity to least-severe P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The fallback for a missing/unknown severity changed from the fail-safe "P1" to the least-severe "P3". Substituted: `severity=undefined` → `SEVERITIES.includes(undefined)` @src/shared/schema.ts:97 → rejects → severity = "P3" @line 99 (base produced "P1"); likewise "critical" or "P5" become P3. Combined with the dropped normalization on lines 97-98, any non-exact-case severity is silently reclassified to the lowest severity with no error or signal, understating findings in the emitted ReviewResult/RawReview output (public schema contract).

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing for spawned codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed block built `env = { ...process.env }` and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_API_TOKEN, then passed it as `env` to `spawnSync`. With both the sanitized object and the `env` option gone, `spawnSync` falls back to its default of inheriting `process.env` verbatim, so the nested `codex exec` agent process (which is LLM-driven and writes its own output) now receives live GitHub credentials it was deliberately denied. Any prompt-influenced child behavior or env-reading tool in that subprocess can exfiltrate the token, and the model's generated output can carry it back to the caller.

findings.title: Restore fork guard before untrusted PRs run on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The job now runs on the `self-hosted` runner for every `pull_request` event, including PRs from forks. The workflow checks out the PR head SHA (`ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, line 23) and then executes fork-controlled code: `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` runs the fork's dependency lifecycle scripts (line 28) and `tsx src/cli.ts ...` runs the fork's own source (line 34). Removing `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` deletes the only control that restricted this to same-repo PRs, so any external contributor's PR can achieve arbitrary code execution on the self-hosted infrastructure (which typically holds persistent state and higher-trust credentials than a GitHub-hosted runner). This is a supply-chain/security regression, not a style change.

findings.title: Zero-valued runner timer overrides are silently replaced by defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard tightens from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0`, so the previously-accepted value `0` now returns `fallbackMs` instead of `0`. Both module constants feed this parser with operator-controlled env vars (lines 3-10): `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0` (previously = escalate to SIGKILL immediately after SIGTERM) is now replaced by the 5000ms default, and `NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0` (previously = stop waiting immediately after SIGKILL) is replaced by the 2000ms default. An explicit operator override is thus silently ignored and escalation/waiting is delayed by up to the default, with no warning. The exported helper `readRunnerDurationMs(value, fallback)` likewise now returns the fallback for the valid input `"0"`, so any external caller asking for a 0ms duration silently gets the default instead.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so unmapped changed files get reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge now uses only the top MAX_HOTSPOTS (6) hotspots returned by the map pass. The deleted block appended a 'tail-coverage' hotspot containing every changedFiles path not present in any selected hotspot's files. With it gone, any changed file the map pass did not assign to a hotspot is never deep-reviewed and never appears in checked[]; the loop at line 97 only covers selected hotspots. The map pass runs without diff text (mapBundle has no patch), so it cannot substitute for the deep review. Result: for large PRs (>30000 patch chars or >10 files) a changed file can be reviewed by nobody while the run still returns a verdict, including PASS.

findings.title: Propagate deep-pass residual risks instead of hardcoding empty
findings.whyItBreaks: The residuals accumulator was removed and candidateMerged.residual_risks is now hardcoded to []. Each deep pass still returns residual_risks (RawReview), but they are no longer collected, so the serialized candidateMerged fed into the critic prompt ({{FINDINGS}}, line 116) and the final deriveVerdict(pruned.findings, pruned.residual_risks) (line 122) can no longer see them. Deep-pass residual risks that carry blocks:true (e.g. 'could not verify X') are therefore dropped from the pipeline, so a blocking uncertainty can be downgraded to a clean verdict, including PASS. Same-shape swallow as the removed catch that used to emit blocks:true for an unreviewed hotspot.

findings.title: Restore focus/deep in the large-review map bundle
findings.whyItBreaks: At base the large-PR path handed `bundle.focus` and `bundle.deep` to the map pass via `mapBundle`, letting the blast-radius survey honor the caller's review focus. After this change the map pass receives only baseSha/headSha/patchStat/changedFiles/agentsMd, so `focus`/`deep` are silently ignored for every large PR, while `reviewSmall` still forwards them (it JSON-stringifies the whole bundle). The same request therefore behaves differently depending on `isLarge()`: focus narrows a 9-file review but is a no-op on a 10-file review.

findings.title: Substitute {{FOCUS}} again or remove it from deep.md
findings.whyItBreaks: `deep.md` is unchanged by this PR (patchStat shows only src/core/review.ts changed, 3 deletions), so it still contains the `{{FOCUS}}` placeholder that base code filled in. Removing the `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` call leaves a raw `{{FOCUS}}` token in the prompt sent to the model, so the deep pass loses the caller's focus directive and receives a template marker instead — a promise (focus is injected) vs implementation (no injection) mismatch.

findings.title: formatDuration can render '1m 60s' after independent seconds rounding
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code computes minutes = Math.floor(ms / 60000) and seconds = Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000) as independent values, so the remainder can round up to 60. For ms = 119999: minutes = 1 and seconds = Math.round(59999 / 1000) = 60, yielding '1m 60s' (the base version returned the correct '2m 0s' by rounding total seconds first and then carrying with totalSeconds % 60). The same class of output occurs for any ms whose ms % 60000 >= 59500 ('1m 60s'), and for 59500..59999 with minutes = 0 ('60s' instead of '1m 0s').

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, contradicting its name and error
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate was changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so the guard rejects only negatives. `parsePositiveInteger("0")` now returns 0 instead of throwing, and `parsePositiveInteger("")`/`parsePositiveInteger("   ")` also return 0 because Number() coerces empty/whitespace to 0. The exported carrier still promises stricter behavior: the function is named parsePositiveInteger (@src/shared/runner.ts:30) and it throws `${label} requires a positive integer` (@src/shared/runner.ts:33). An exported validation contract that promises a positive integer but returns 0/silent-0-for-empty breaks that contract for every eventual caller, and notably converts a previously-signalled empty/invalid input into a legitimate-looking 0.
